dimensions.gloss: Whether a disclosure of AI use or authorship involvement was actually made for a given case (yes/no/not stated), as an outcome rather than a policy requirement.
dimensions.note: "not stated" carries an example quote that does not obviously match it (figure-type classification); it is grouped here as the closest fit to a completion-state value, but this is a close call.

dimensions.gloss: Transparency invoked as a general normative virtue underlying responsible disclosure, not a specific named reporting field.
dimensions.note: Kept separate from any "transparency" used as a named checklist field, per the rule that the vague-virtue sense and the named-field sense are different axes; only the virtue sense occurred in this batch.

dimensions.canonical_label: Approval and accountability for the work
dimensions.gloss: Who signs off on the final version and remains answerable for the work as a whole, whether framed as an ICMJE-style authorship criterion, a general responsibility principle, or a regulatory remedy requirement.
dimensions.note: Merges narrow authorship-criteria language ("final approval", "accountability") with broader responsibility/remedy language from non-authorship schemes; treated as the same axis (who answers for the work) but this spans different scheme families.

dimensions.canonical_label: Task or stage of AI/contributor involvement
dimensions.gloss: Which task, activity, or stage of the work (writing, analysis, literature review, coding, drafting, administrative work, etc.) AI or a contributor was involved in.
dimensions.note: "activity classes" comes from a software-provenance ontology rather than a manuscript checklist, and bare "ai" is a weak, generic label included because its example values are themselves task names; both are close calls.

dimensions.gloss: The stated reason or goal for which AI was used, reported as a field distinct from which task-stage it was used in.
Where in the output or venue the disclosure statement must or does appear: a specific manuscript section (title, abstract, methods...) or a publication channel (public vs. cover letter).
dimensions.note: Merges "which manuscript section" placement with "public vs. private channel" placement as the same underlying location axis; treated as one axis but this is a close call.

dimensions.gloss: What type of substantive contribution or role (author, writer, editor, a CRediT category, an ICMJE substantial-contribution criterion) a party performed.
variants: conception or design of the work
acquisition, analysis or interpretation of the data for the work
dimensions.note: "a (disclosure and role clarity)" is a governance-checkpoint label folded in as a close call because its substance is about clarifying who did what.

dimensions.gloss: Whether the chain of origin of content or a claim can be traced back to its source, ranging from no traceability to full, independently verifiable logs.
Whether the materials needed to reproduce the AI-assisted work (prompts, parameters, input/output data, code) are disclosed or archived.
dimensions.note: Prompt-sharing folded in as a close call, since prompts are one specific kind of reproducibility material named separately by some schemes.

dimensions.gloss: The mechanics of how credit is assigned among contributors (author selection, order, listings, acknowledgements), as distinct from what task a contributor performed.
Whose consent or authorization was obtained, and how, for the use of a person's data, likeness, or contribution.
The substantive-content dimension of a contribution, named as one of two independent dimensions (content vs. form) by its source framework.
dimensions.note: The example values (source files, docs, commit messages) sit oddly with the content/form quote; kept as its own singleton rather than merged with "form", since the source explicitly frames them as two separate dimensions.

dimensions.gloss: The stylistic/formal dimension of how AI involvement is marked (e.g., source references, visual indicators such as logos or watermarks), named as distinct from substantive "content".
dimensions.note: Example values look closer to a disclosure-format axis than to a content/form contrast, but kept separate from "content" per the source's explicit two-dimensions framing.

dimensions.canonical_label: Fairness and equity of AI access
dimensions.gloss: Whether the disclosure or policy addresses equitable access to AI and fair treatment across users, as distinct from technical accessibility of data or code.
A general, catch-all field for ethical considerations of AI use, named alongside but not specific to privacy, consent, or bias.
How much human review, checking, or verification was applied to AI output, ranging from none to full independent validation.
dimensions.note: "5 (iv)" (human-AI interaction and expertise in data handling) is folded in as a close call, since it concerns the nature of interaction as much as the extent of review.

dimensions.gloss: How much of the output AI produced or how deeply it was involved, usually expressed as an ordered scale, tier, or dichotomy.
dimensions.note: "a three-category typology" (novel production / error-correcting reconstruction / format conversion) and "a responsible reliance spectrum" (risk-framed) characterize AI's role by type or risk rather than pure quantity; included as close calls.

dimensions.gloss: Disclosure of the limitations or caveats associated with using AI in the work.
Whether privacy or data-protection considerations of AI use are disclosed.

dimensions.canonical_label: Timing of AI use in the workflow
dimensions.gloss: When, relative to the human's own independent effort, AI was used (before, during, or after).
Whether AI use is framed as an academic-integrity/honesty concern, named as its own component distinct from AI-literacy or accountability.
Whether and how AI may be used by reviewers within the peer-review process itself.
The degree of self-determination or independent agency preserved for the human party affected by AI use.
The declared limits on what AI was allowed to do, reported as a field distinct from stage-of-use and purpose.
Whether AI-generated or AI-assisted content of a given output type (code/data, images/figures) is permitted, permitted with conditions, or prohibited.
Whether and how the underlying data, code, or metadata can be found and accessed, including retrieval protocol, authentication, access conditions, and access dates.
variants: a1.1 free, open, universal retrieval protocol
dimensions.note: The four FAIR-style "A1/A1.1/A1.2/A2" accessibility sub-items are folded into this broader axis as a specific accessibility sub-scheme.

dimensions.gloss: Whether a venue's policy mandates, encourages, or leaves optional the disclosure of AI use, and whether supporting infrastructure (templates, guideline sections) exists.
Whether AI-generated or synthetic content is clearly marked and distinguished from human-produced or real-world content.
A meta-label naming a scheme's own top-level set of categories, domains, or items, rather than a single comparable disclosure axis in itself.
dimensions.note: Residual/structural grouping: each of these four labels points to a different checklist's internal list of categories rather than a shared axis; grouping them together is itself a close call.

dimensions.gloss: Whether a named author received credit without having contributed substantially to the work.
The identity of the AI tool or system used, including its name, version, type (generative vs. assistive), and any changes made to it during the study.
dimensions.note: "tools" (a generative-vs-assistive functional classification) is a somewhat looser fit than the pure identity/version fields; included as a close call.

dimensions.gloss: The degree of independence from funding or industry influence of a cited source.
The intended application, setting, and integration of an AI system within a real-world workflow, such as a clinical pathway.
Which parties (e.g., model providers, detection-tool providers) a verifier is required to trust when using content-transparency mechanisms.
Reporting of any analysis of the AI system's performance errors and how those errors were identified.
Whether an AI system's feedback or monitoring is delivered on-demand or continuously in real time.
Whether an AI system's messages are framed reflectively, as inquiry, or suggestively, as a directive.
The confidence and role an AI system displays toward the user, from humble/uncertain to authoritative/objective.
The inclusion/exclusion criteria applied, at the level of participants or of input data, to an AI intervention's evaluation.
How input data for the AI intervention were acquired and selected, and how poor-quality or unavailable input data were handled.

dimensions.canonical_label: AI output and its role in decisions
dimensions.gloss: What the AI intervention's output is and how it contributed to downstream decision-making or clinical practice.
Whether an AI system's interpretations are fixed as fact or can be reflected on, revised, or rejected by the user.

dimensions.canonical_label: AI system's information disclosure to users
dimensions.gloss: How much sensor-based or contextual information an AI system surfaces to its end-users, from implicit context only to explicit raw signals.
The factual correctness of content and its alignment with the underlying data.
The specific, measurable action taken within an AI-assisted workflow, such as an acknowledgment, override, or escalation.
Whether a venue's AI guidelines are stated to be subject to future update or revision.
Whether the acting party in a given step is classified as human, AI, or tool, and which type of agent is being substituted or compared.
Whether an AI system can be credited or listed as an author or co-author of the work.
variants: ai applications cannot be listed as authors.

dimensions.gloss: How AI's fundamental nature or role is conceived (e.g., a bounded supportive tool, a contamination risk, socio-technical infrastructure), as distinct from how much it was used.
variants: ai as supportive but bounded tool

dimensions.gloss: Whether a quality-assessment framework includes a dimension for assessing competence in using AI.
Whether a venue uses automated detection tools to screen submissions for undisclosed AI-generated content.
The technical infrastructure (compliance platforms, AI gateways, runtime layers) used to enforce AI governance rules.
Whether a framework names literacy about AI's limitations as its own distinct competency, separate from academic-integrity norms.
A venue's overall stance toward AI use itself (welcomed, permitted, discouraged), as distinct from whether disclosure of that use is required.
